mainTopic: How the תנא קמא and רבי אלעזר read the פסוקים about a self-seller versus a slave sold by בית דין, and which תנא rejects the 'שכיר' 'שכיר' גזירה שוה
overview: The גמרא looks at a מחלוקת between the תנא קמא and רבי אלעזר about a man who sold himself as a slave (מוכר עצמו) and a man sold by בית דין. First, using the pattern 'ואידך?', it shows how each side uses the words of the פסוק about רציעה: 'אזנו', 'העבד', and the right-ear גזירה שוה. Next it does the same for the הענקה (severance gift). For the תנא קמא, the word 'לו' leaves out the self-seller. For רבי אלעזר, it keeps the slave's creditor from taking the gift, a point that matters only if one follows רבי נתן. Then it turns to the שפחה כנענית: 'לו' either leaves out the self-seller or teaches that the master can give her even against the slave's will. Here the גמרא explains that the slave's 'night work' is living with the שפחה. The גמרא then searches for a תנא who rejects the 'שכיר' 'שכיר' גזירה שוה. It tries רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, but רב נחמן בר יצחק shows that this proof does not hold. Along the way it explains why the תורה had to teach both that יובל frees the court-sold slave and that it frees the נרצע, and why 'לעולם' means until יובל. Finally it names רבי as the תנא and begins quoting his ברייתא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The other תנא uses 'ear' for a comparison
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the other תנא (רבי אלעזר) does with the word 'אזנו', and answers that he needs it for a גזירה שוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other תנא, what does he do with this word? That word comes for a גזירה שוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The תנא קמא used the word 'אזנו' to teach that one who sold himself is not pierced. The גמרא asks how the other תנא, who disagrees, uses that word, and answers: for a גזירה שוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a word in the תורה is not wasted. Since the other תנא does not learn the תנא קמא's rule from 'אזנו', he must be using it for something else. The answer: the word 'ear' links this פסוק to another פסוק that also says 'ear'.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one: what does the other opinion do with this word?
A comparison between two פסוקים that share the same word
That one (that word)
That comes (to teach)

steps.confusionAlert: 'ואידך?' is not an attack. It is the גמרא asking, 'How does the other side use this פסוק?' You will see it again and again in this passage, each time switching to the other תנא.

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: The other תנא, who says even one who sold himself gets pierced. What does he do with the word 'his ear'?

phrases.english: That word comes for a verbal comparison.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידָּךְ? הָהִיא – לִגְזֵירָה שָׁוָה הוּא דַּאֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the back-and-forth by explaining how the other תנא uses the word that the תנא קמא relied on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the other תנא learn from 'אזנו'?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He uses the word 'ear' for a גזירה שוה.

steps.title: The ברייתא: piercing is on the right ear
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא of רבי אליעזר learns from the word 'ear' that the piercing must be on the right ear, by comparing it to the מצורע.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר says, from where do we know that the piercing is on the right ear? It says 'ear' here and 'ear' there. Just as there it is the right ear, so too here it is the right ear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show which גזירה שוה it means. 'Ear' by the slave is compared to 'ear' by the purification of a מצורע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the slave, the תורה just says 'ear' and does not say which one. By the מצורע, the פסוק says 'the right ear'. Since both use the same word, we learn that the slave is pierced on the right ear too.

keyTerms.meaning: Piercing the ear of a עבד עברי who wants to stay with his master
The right ear
Here (by the slave)
There (by the מצורע)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is why, in practice, a עבד עברי is pierced on his right ear.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא: רבי אליעזר says:
From where do we know that the piercing is on the right ear?
It says here: 'ear',
and it says there: 'ear'.
phrases.notes: 'There' is the מצורע's purification, ויקרא 14:14.

phrases.english: Just as there it is the right one,
so too here it is the right one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the גזירה שוה mentioned in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That the word 'ear' is used for a גזירה שוה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי אליעזר comparing the slave's ear to the מצורע's right ear

steps.title: The תנא קמא: why 'his ear' and not just 'ear'?
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא answers that for the comparison, plain 'ear' would be enough. The extra 'his' in 'אזנו' is free to teach his own rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? If so, let the פסוק say 'ear'. Why does it say 'his ear'?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא switches back to the תנא קמא. It explains that he also accepts the גזירה שוה, but he still finds something extra in the word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison only needs the word 'ear'. The ending 'his' (the letter ו in אזנו) is extra. The תנא קמא uses that extra part to teach that one who sold himself is not pierced.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Let the פסוק say
His ear

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: Now we're back to the תנא קמא: how does he handle this?

phrases.english: If so, let the verse say 'ear';
what is 'his ear'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ? אִם כֵּן לֵימָא קְרָא ״אֹזֶן״, מַאי ״אׇזְנוֹ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers for the תנא קמא how he can keep his derivation even though the word is also used for the גזירה שוה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Ear' gives the גזירה שוה, and the extra 'his' teaches the תנא קמא's rule.

steps.title: The other תנא: 'his ear' excludes a maidservant
steps.stepSummary: The other תנא needs the word 'his' to teach that a man is pierced but not a woman (an אמה).
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He needs that word to teach: 'his ear', and not her ear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא switches to the other תנא again. It explains that he also uses the extra 'his', but for a different rule: a maidservant is not pierced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'His' is a male word. So for this תנא, 'his ear' means a male slave is pierced and a female slave (אמה) is not. That uses up the extra word, so he has nothing left to exclude one who sold himself.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it (for something else)
Her ear

phrases.english: And the other one?
He needs that word for:
'his ear', and not her ear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds for the other תנא, explaining what he learns from the extra 'his'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'His ear' teaches that an אמה is not pierced.

steps.title: The תנא קמא learns 'not a maidservant' from 'the slave'
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא gets the rule that an אמה is not pierced from a different word: 'העבד', 'the slave'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He learns it from 'And if the slave says': the slave, and not a maidservant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the תנא קמא. It asks how he knows a maidservant is not pierced, since he used 'his' for something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'העבד', a male slave. The תנא קמא learns from that word that an אמה is excluded. So he does not need 'his ear' for that rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He learns it from
The (male) slave
A Jewish maidservant

phrases.english: And the other one?
He learns it from 'And if the slave says':
phrases.notes: שמות 21:5

phrases.english: the slave, and not a maidservant.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ? נָפְקָא לַהּ מִ״וְּאִם יֹאמַר הָעֶבֶד״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the תנא קמא gets the 'not an אמה' rule from another source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: From 'העבד': a slave, not a maidservant.

steps.title: The other תנא: he must ask while still a slave
steps.stepSummary: The other תנא needs 'ואם יאמר העבד' for a different rule: the request to stay must be made while he is still a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He needs it to teach that he must say it while he is still a slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא switches back to the other תנא. It explains that he does not learn 'not a maidservant' from 'העבד', because he needs that word for another rule. The next step asks how the תנא קמא gets this same rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For him, 'if the slave says' teaches about timing. He must ask to stay while he is still a slave, not after he has gone free. This raises a new question: where does the תנא קמא get this timing rule? Steps 7-8 answer it.

keyTerms.meaning: Only if he says
While he is (still) a slave

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides accept the right-ear גזירה שוה. The תנא קמא: 'his' excludes one who sold himself, and 'the slave' excludes an אמה. The other תנא: 'his' excludes an אמה, and 'the slave' teaches that he must ask while still a slave.

phrases.english: And the other one?
He needs it for:
that he must say it while he is still a slave.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ? מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ: עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר כְּשֶׁהוּא עֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the other תנא's use of 'העבד', which raises the question in step 7 of where the תנא קמא learns this rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Every word in the פסוק is used by each side, so the מחלוקת about one who sold himself stands consistently.

steps.title: Where the first תנא learns 'while still a slave'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the תנא קמא knows the slave must ask while still a slave, and answers that he learns it from 'עבד' versus 'העבד'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He learns it from the difference between 'slave' and 'the slave'.
steps.whatsHappening: The other תנא used 'ואם יאמר העבד' for the rule that he must ask while still a slave. So the גמרא asks where the תנא קמא gets that rule, since he already used 'העבד' for the אמה rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא gets two rules out of the word. Plain 'עבד' would already teach that he must ask while still a slave. The extra ה in 'העבד' adds a second rule: an עבד is pierced but an אמה is not.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one? It asks how the other side handles a rule or a word.
'Slave' and 'the slave'. The extra letter ה is used to teach an extra rule.
It comes out from, meaning he derives it from

phrases.english: And the other?
phrases.notes: Here 'the other' is the תנא קמא, who already used העבד to teach that an אמה is not pierced.

phrases.english: He derives it from 'slave' versus 'the slave.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns step 6's rule back onto the תנא קמא and asks for his source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תנא קמא learns both rules from 'עבד' versus 'העבד'.

steps.title: The other תנא does not learn from 'the slave'
steps.stepSummary: The other תנא does not learn anything from the difference between 'עבד' and 'העבד', so he needs the whole phrase for one rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He does not expound 'slave' versus 'the slave.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the other תנא cannot use the same trick. He simply does not learn from the extra ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the word-by-word exchange. The two תנאים disagree about how to read the words. The תנא קמא draws a lesson from the extra ה. The other תנא does not, so he needs 'אזנו' for the אמה rule and 'העבד' for the 'still a slave' rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not expound, meaning he learns no lesson from this wording

steps.whatToRemember: Every word got used. The תנא קמא learns two rules from 'העבד' and uses 'אזנו' for his own rule. The other תנא does not learn from the extra ה, so he uses 'אזנו' to teach 'not an אמה'.

phrases.english: And the other?
Does not expound 'slave' versus 'the slave.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the other תנא cannot use step 7's reading.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two sides disagree on whether to learn from 'עבד' versus 'העבד', and that explains how each one uses the words.

steps.title: Why a self-seller gets no severance gift
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new point: what is the source of the תנא קמא that a man who sells himself does not get a הענקה?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the first תנא, who says that one who sells himself is not given a severance gift?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a second disagreement in the same ברייתא, about the הענקה. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says only a slave sold by בית דין gets a הענקה. A man who sold himself does not. The גמרא wants the פסוק behind this limit.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed תנא in a ברייתא
A man who sold himself as a slave because he was poor
Giving the freed slave a parting gift

phrases.english: What is the reason of the first tanna
who says that one who sells himself
is not given a severance gift?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the piercing debate to the הענקה debate.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that keeps a self-seller from getting a הענקה.

steps.title: 'To him' leaves out the self-seller
steps.stepSummary: The word 'לו' in 'הענק תעניק לו' limits the gift to the slave sold by בית דין, so not one who sold himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה limited it in the case of one sold by בית דין: 'You shall surely give him a severance gift.' 'To him', but not to one who sells himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'לו', 'to him', narrows the gift to the slave sold by בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is talking about a thief whom בית דין sold. 'לו' is read as 'only to this kind of slave'. That leaves out a man who sold himself.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah narrowed or excluded something
A thief who was sold by the court to pay back what he stole
'To him'. Here it is read as limiting the rule.

phrases.english: The Merciful One excluded
regarding one sold by the court:
'You shall surely give a severance gift to him'
phrases.notes: דברים 15:14

phrases.english: 'to him,' but not to one who sells himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיעֵט רַחֲמָנָא גַּבֵּי מְכָרוּהוּ בֵּית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'לו' limits the הענקה to a slave sold by בית דין.

steps.title: The other תנא: 'to him, not his heirs'
steps.stepSummary: The other תנא gives a self-seller a gift too, so he needs 'לו' for something else. The first suggestion is: not to his heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He needs that word for: 'to him', but not to his heirs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the other תנא does with 'לו'. It suggests he uses it to say the gift does not go to the slave's heirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other תנא gives a הענקה even to a man who sold himself, so 'לו' is not limiting that. The suggestion is that it means: if the slave dies, his heirs do not get the gift.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it for, meaning he uses this word for a different lesson
His heirs

phrases.english: And the other?
phrases.notes: He gives a gift even to a man who sold himself. So what does he do with 'to him'?

phrases.english: He needs that for:
'to him,' but not to his heirs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the other תנא uses the word from step 10.

steps.title: A slave is like a hired worker, so his heirs should get it
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is attacked. The תורה calls the slave a 'שכיר', and a worker's pay goes to his heirs. So the gift should go to his heirs too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why shouldn't his heirs get it? The תורה called him a 'hired worker'. Just as a hired worker's wages go to his heirs, so too this one's wages should go to his heirs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the 'not his heirs' reading. A slave is compared to a שכיר, and a שכיר's earnings pass to his heirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הענקה is treated like payment for the slave's work. Unpaid wages are owed to a worker's heirs if he dies. So it makes no sense to say the heirs lose the gift.

keyTerms.meaning: A hired worker
His wages, the pay for his work
Why not?

phrases.english: Why not his heirs?
The Merciful One called him a 'hired worker,'
phrases.notes: דברים 15:18

phrases.english: just as a hired worker's wages go to his heirs,
so too this one's wages go to his heirs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the suggestion in step 11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A slave is called a שכיר. A שכיר's wages go to his heirs, so the gift should go to them too.

steps.title: 'To him, not to his creditor'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new reading: 'לו' means the gift goes to the slave himself and not to someone he owes money to.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: 'to him', but not to his creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The heirs reading is dropped. The גמרא now says 'לו' teaches that the slave's creditor cannot grab the gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heirs do get the gift, because they stand in his place. A lender is different. He cannot take the gift as payment for the slave's debt, because the תורה gives it 'to him'.

keyTerms.meaning: His creditor, someone the slave owes money to
Rather. It drops the earlier idea and gives a new one.

steps.whatToRemember: For the other תנא, 'לו' means the creditor cannot take the gift. For the תנא קמא, it means a man who sold himself gets none.

phrases.english: Rather: 'to him,' but not to his creditor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces step 11's reading after the challenge in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reading of the word in the פסוק

steps.title: Why the creditor needs to be excluded: רבי נתן's rule
steps.stepSummary: Excluding the creditor is needed because we follow רבי נתן. He says a lender can collect directly from his borrower's debtor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since we generally hold like רבי נתן, as it was taught: רבי נתן said: from where do we know that if one man is owed a מנה by his fellow, and that fellow is owed the same by another, we take from this last one and give to the first? The verse says: 'And he shall give to the one he wronged.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why a פסוק is needed to keep the creditor away. Without it, רבי נתן's rule would let him take the gift straight from the master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי נתן's rule, money owed to the borrower can be taken by the lender directly. The master owes the slave the הענקה. So the slave's lender could collect it straight from the master. 'לו' teaches that this rule does not apply to the הענקה.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who is owed money, a lender
A sum of one hundred זוז
In general, in other cases
The פסוק teaches

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the הענקה belongs to the slave himself. The Torah makes it an exception to the usual rule of רבי נתן.

phrases.english: Since we generally hold
like Rabbi Natan,
as it was taught: Rabbi Natan said:
From where do we know, for one who is owed a maneh by his fellow,
and his fellow is owed by another fellow,
phrases.notes: The words 'is owed a מנה' are left out here, but they carry over from the line before.

phrases.english: from where do we know that we take from this one
and give to that one?
The verse teaches:
'And he shall give to the one he wronged.'
phrases.notes: במדבר 5:7

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the reading in step 13 is needed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without 'לו', רבי נתן's rule would let the slave's lender collect the הענקה straight from the master.

steps.title: So 'לו' comes to exclude the creditor
steps.stepSummary: Because we might have followed רבי נתן, the word 'לו' is needed to keep the gift away from the slave's creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why 'to him' comes to exclude the creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the point from the last step. Since רבי נתן would let a creditor collect straight from the master, 'לו' is needed to block that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי נתן's rule, the creditor could have taken the gift directly from the master. The word 'לו' tells us the gift must reach the slave himself. This finishes the other תנא's use of 'לו'.

keyTerms.meaning: to exclude, to leave something out

phrases.english: "To him" comes to exclude.
phrases.notes: It excludes the slave's creditor, who might otherwise have collected the gift from the master directly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the reasoning of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'לו' excludes the creditor, which is needed because of רבי נתן.

steps.title: Why the first תנא doesn't need this
steps.stepSummary: The first תנא doesn't need a פסוק to exclude the creditor, because we don't hold like רבי נתן anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other תנא? In general we don't hold like רבי נתן either.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the first תנא handles the creditor problem, since he used 'לו' for something else. It answers that he simply doesn't follow רבי נתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first תנא used 'לו' to exclude a self-seller from the gift. He doesn't need 'לו' for the creditor, because without רבי נתן's rule a creditor can't collect from the master in the first place. So no verse is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: and the other one (how does the other opinion deal with this?)
in general, everywhere else
we do not hold this way

steps.whatToRemember: One תנא uses 'לו' to exclude a self-seller from the gift. The other uses it to exclude a creditor, and that use only matters if you follow רבי נתן.

phrases.english: And the other?
phrases.notes: This is the first תנא, who used 'לו' to leave the self-seller out of the gift.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָלְמָא נָמֵי לָא סְבִירָא לַן כְּרַבִּי נָתָן.
phrases.english: Generally too, we do not hold like רבי נתן.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ? בְּעָלְמָא נָמֵי לָא סְבִירָא לַן כְּרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the opposing תנא doesn't need the creditor exclusion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the first תנא deals with the creditor without using 'לו'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He rejects רבי נתן's rule, so there is nothing to exclude.

steps.title: Why no שפחה כנענית for a self-seller?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the first תנא's rule that a master does not give a self-seller a שפחה כנענית.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the first תנא, who says that if a man sold himself, his master does not give him a Canaanite maidservant?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about a different difference between a self-seller and one sold by בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the topic was the gift (הענקה). Now the topic is the שפחה כנענית. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק the first תנא uses to leave the self-seller out.

keyTerms.meaning: the first opinion stated in a ברייתא or משנה
a man who sold himself as a slave because he was poor
a non-Jewish maidservant
gives him

phrases.english: What is the reason of the first תנא
who says that one who sells himself,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the gift to a second difference: the שפחה כנענית.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for leaving a self-seller out of the שפחה כנענית.

steps.title: 'לו' in the פסוק of the wife
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'אם אדניו יתן לו אשה' is about one sold by בית דין, and 'לו' means only him and not a self-seller.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה limited it when speaking about one sold by בית דין: 'If his master gives him a wife.' 'To him', and not to one who sells himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The word 'לו' in the פסוק about the master giving a wife limits the rule to the slave sold by בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works the same way as the gift: the פסוק is talking about a slave sold by בית דין. The extra word 'לו' shows that only he gets a שפחה כנענית, not someone who sold himself.

keyTerms.meaning: the Torah limited it (left something out)
בית דין sold him (because he stole and couldn't pay)

phrases.aramaic: מַיעֵט רַחֲמָנָא גַּבֵּי מְכָרוּהוּ בֵּית דִּין:
phrases.english: The Torah limited it regarding one sold by בית דין:
"If his master gives him a wife"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:4

phrases.english: "to him", and not to one who sells himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַיעֵט רַחֲמָנָא גַּבֵּי מְכָרוּהוּ בֵּית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'לו' in 'אם אדניו יתן לו אשה' excludes the self-seller.

steps.title: The other opinion: 'לו' means against his will
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר, who gives a self-seller a שפחה too, reads 'לו' as 'even against his will'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other? 'To him' means even against his will.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the other opinion uses the word 'לו'. He reads it as teaching that the master can give the slave the שפחה even if the slave doesn't want her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר can't use 'לו' to exclude a self-seller, because he holds a self-seller also gets a שפחה. So he uses 'לו' for a different lesson: the slave is given the שפחה whether he likes it or not.

keyTerms.meaning: against his will

phrases.english: And the other?
phrases.notes: This is רבי אלעזר, who says even a self-seller gets a שפחה.

phrases.english: "To him": against his will.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other opinion's reading of the same word.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'לו' teaches that the master gives the שפחה even against the slave's will.

steps.title: The first תנא learns 'against his will' from another פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The first תנא learns that the שפחה is given against the slave's will from 'כי משנה שכר שכיר'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other? He learns it from 'For double the hire of a hired worker.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where the first תנא gets the 'against his will' rule, since he used 'לו' for something else. He learns it from a different פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree the שפחה can be given against the slave's will. They only disagree about which פסוק teaches it. The first תנא uses 'כי משנה שכר שכיר', explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: it comes out (is learned) from
a hired worker

phrases.english: And the other?

phrases.english: He learns it from "for double the hire of a hired worker,"
phrases.notes: דברים 15:18

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ? מִ״כִּי מִשְׁנֶה שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר״ נָפְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the first תנא has another source for 'against his will'.

steps.title: The ברייתא: a slave works day and night
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads 'double the hire of a hired worker' to mean a hired worker works by day, but a Hebrew slave works day and night.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'For double the hire of a hired worker he served you.' A hired worker works only by day; a Hebrew slave works both by day and by night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show how this פסוק is read. The 'double' means the slave works both day and night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave is worth 'double' a hired worker because he works at night too. What that night work is has not been explained yet. The next steps will clear it up.

keyTerms.meaning: double
a Hebrew (Jewish) slave

phrases.english: As it was taught:
"For double the hire of a hired worker he served you":
a hired worker works only by day,

phrases.aramaic: עֶבֶד עִבְרִי עוֹבֵד בֵּין בַּיּוֹם וּבֵין בַּלַּיְלָה.
phrases.english: a Hebrew slave works both by day and by night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 20 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That 'כי משנה שכר שכיר' teaches something about the slave beyond a hired worker.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא explaining the 'double' as day and night work.

steps.title: Can a slave really work day and night?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: the תורה says the slave must live as well as his master, so how can he work all night?
steps.simpleTranslation: Could you really think that a Hebrew slave works by day and by night? Doesn't it already say 'because he is well off with you', meaning with you in food and with you in drink?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's statement. Working day and night doesn't fit the תורה's demand that the slave be treated as well as his master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'כי טוב לו עמך' teaches the slave must eat and drink like his master. A master who must treat him that well can't make him work all night with no rest. So 'night work' must mean something else.

keyTerms.meaning: could it enter your mind? (meaning: that can't be right)
but isn't it already said?
because he is well off with you

phrases.english: Could it enter your mind

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁעֶבֶד עִבְרִי עוֹבֵד בֵּין בַּיּוֹם וּבֵין בַּלַּיְלָה?
phrases.english: that a Hebrew slave works both by day and by night?

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר: ״כִּי טוֹב לוֹ עִמָּךְ״ –
phrases.english: Isn't it already said: "Because he is well off with you":
phrases.notes: דברים 15:16

phrases.english: with you in food, with you in drink.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the plain meaning of the ברייתא's 'day and night'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a Hebrew slave works day and night.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah requires the slave to live as well as his master, which doesn't fit forcing him to work all night.

steps.title: The night work is the שפחה כנענית
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק explains that the 'night work' is that the master gives the slave a שפחה כנענית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: From here we learn that his master gives him a Canaanite maidservant.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers the challenge. The 'night work' isn't hard labor; it's being given a שפחה כנענית whose children belong to the master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the ברייתא fits the תורה's demand that the slave be treated well. Because this is called 'work' for the master, it is done even against the slave's will. That is how the first תנא learns 'בעל כרחו' without using 'לו'.

keyTerms.meaning: from here (we learn)

steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions agree the שפחה כנענית can be given against the slave's will. The first תנא learns it from 'משנה שכר שכיר' (night work = שפחה), so 'לו' is free to exclude a self-seller. רבי אלעזר learns it from 'לו'.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'works day and night' as hard labor around the clock. The גמרא rejects that reading; the night 'work' is the שפחה כנענית.

phrases.english: And רבי יצחק said:

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן שֶׁרַבּוֹ מוֹסֵר לוֹ שִׁפְחָה כְּנַעֲנִית.
phrases.english: From here we learn that his master gives him a Canaanite maidservant.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: מִכָּאן שֶׁרַבּוֹ מוֹסֵר לוֹ שִׁפְחָה כְּנַעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: 'night work' means the שפחה כנענית, not physical labor.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The slave does real labor all night, which would clash with 'כי טוב לו עמך'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The night work is living with the שפחה כנענית, which is done even against his will.

steps.title: Why רבי אלעזר still needs the word ׳לו׳
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר does not rely only on ׳משנה שכר שכיר׳. From that פסוק alone we might think the master can give a שפחה only with the slave's consent, so ׳לו׳ teaches that he can do it even against the slave's will.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other (רבי אלעזר)? If we learned it only from there, I would have said this applies only when the slave agrees, but against his will, no. So ׳לו׳ teaches us that it applies even against his will.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רבי אלעזר deals with the פסוק the first תנא used. It answers that this פסוק alone would not teach that the master can do it against the slave's will.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first תנא learned ׳against his will׳ from ׳משנה שכר שכיר׳. רבי אלעזר says that this פסוק only shows that a שפחה can be given at all, and maybe only with the slave's agreement. The extra word ׳לו׳ is what adds ׳even against his will׳.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one, meaning what does the other opinion say about this?
With his consent
Against his will
It teaches us (something we would not have known)

phrases.english: And the other?
phrases.notes: This means רבי אלעזר. How does he deal with ׳משנה שכר שכיר׳, the פסוק the first תנא used?

phrases.english: If it were only from there,
I would have said: this applies only with his consent,
but against his will, I would say no;
so it teaches us.
phrases.notes: The word ׳לו׳ teaches that it applies even against his will.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the argument between רבי אלעזר and the first תנא in steps 19-20 and explains רבי אלעזר's side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What רבי אלעזר does with ׳משנה שכר שכיר׳.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: That פסוק alone would suggest only ׳with consent׳. ׳לו׳ is needed to teach ׳even against his will׳.

steps.title: Who does not learn the ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״ link?
steps.stepSummary: Both opinions here accept the link between the two passages that use the word ״שָׂכִיר״. So the גמרא asks which תנא does not accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, who is the תנא who does not learn ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which תנא rejects the ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״ link. This question sets up the next step, which brings a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far, both רבי אלעזר and the first תנא seem to accept the link. Now the גמרא wants to find a תנא who does not use it.

keyTerms.meaning: Learning a law from one passage to another because both use the same word
He learns (one law from another source)
A hired worker, the word that appears in both passages

phrases.english: Rather, who is the תנא
who does not learn ״hired worker״ ״hired worker״?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since both opinions so far accept the link, the גמרא now looks for a תנא who does not.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: יובל frees the slave sold by בית דין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points to a ברייתא. There, רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says ׳ושב אל משפחתו׳ must be teaching that a man sold by בית דין two or three years before יובל goes free at יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is this תנא, as a ברייתא teaches: ׳And he shall return to his family.׳ רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said: What is the פסוק speaking about? If it is about someone who sold himself, that is already stated. If it is about a נרצע, that is already stated. So the פסוק must be speaking about a man sold by בית דין two or three years before יובל: יובל sets him free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the תנא is רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. It quotes his ברייתא, which uses a פסוק to teach that יובל frees a slave sold by בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב rules out the other cases one by one. The self-seller and the נרצע are already covered elsewhere, so the פסוק must be about the slave sold by בית דין. The fact that he needs a פסוק for this case is what the גמרא uses in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A man who sold himself as a slave because he was poor
A slave whose ear was pierced because he chose to stay on
A man sold as a slave by the court
The Jubilee year, every fiftieth year

phrases.english: It is this תנא,
as it was taught in a ברייתא:
״And he shall return to his family, etc.״
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:41

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said:
What is the verse speaking about?

phrases.aramaic: אִי בְּמוֹכֵר עַצְמוֹ – הֲרֵי כְּבָר אָמוּר!
phrases.english: If about one who sold himself, that is already stated!
phrases.notes: The פסוק before it already says that he works only until יובל.

phrases.english: If about a pierced slave, that is already stated!
So the verse must be speaking only
about one whom the court sold
two or three years before the Jubilee,
teaching that the Jubilee sets him free.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25 by naming רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and quoting his ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who needs a separate פסוק to teach that יובל frees the slave sold by בית דין.

steps.title: His need for a פסוק shows he rejects the link
steps.stepSummary: If רבי אליעזר בן יעקב accepted the ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״ link, he could learn the court-sold case from the self-seller. Needing a פסוק suggests that he does not accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you think he learns ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״, why do I need the פסוק? Let him learn it from ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why this ברייתא shows that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב rejects the link: he would not need a separate פסוק if he used it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the link, every rule of the self-seller, including going free at יובל, would carry over to the slave sold by בית דין. Using a פסוק for something he could have learned anyway seems unnecessary, so it looks like he does not accept the link.

keyTerms.meaning: It enters your mind, meaning ׳if you were to think…׳
Why do I need it?

phrases.english: And if it would enter your mind
that he learns ״hired worker״ ״hired worker״,
why do I need it?
phrases.notes: Meaning the פסוק ׳ושב אל משפחתו׳.

phrases.english: Let him learn it from ״hired worker״ ״hired worker״!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ יָלֵיף ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״, לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the ברייתא in step 26 shows that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב rejects the link.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not learn ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״.
steps.raayaSupportSource: His use of a separate פסוק for the court-sold slave going free at יובל.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: the פסוק was needed anyway
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says רבי אליעזר בן יעקב may accept the link. The פסוק was still needed, because without it we might have penalized the court-sold slave, who did a sin, by not freeing him at יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Really, he does learn ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״, and the פסוק was still needed. You might have thought: the self-seller did no sin, but the man sold by בית דין did a sin, so we should penalize him. So the פסוק teaches us that he goes free too.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק pushes back on the proof. He says the פסוק has a different job, so it does not show that the link is rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The link might carry over the self-seller's rule, but we could still have said that a sinner does not get the same benefit. The פסוק blocks that idea of a penalty, so רבי אליעזר בן יעקב can accept the link and still need the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (keeping the original idea)
It was needed
A sin, a forbidden act
Let us penalize him

steps.whatToRemember: Needing a פסוק does not always mean rejecting a גזירה שווה. The פסוק might be there to block a possible penalty for someone who did a sin.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Really, he does learn ״hired worker״ ״hired worker״,
and the verse was still needed,
because it would have entered your mind to say:

phrases.aramaic: מוֹכֵר עַצְמוֹ הוּא, דְּלָא עֲבַד אִיסּוּרָא,
phrases.english: it is the one who sold himself, who did no sin, who goes free,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מְכָרוּהוּ בֵּית דִּין, דַּעֲבַד אִיסּוּרָא,
phrases.english: but one the court sold, who did a sin,
I would say we should penalize him;
so the verse teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: לְעוֹלָם יָלֵיף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 27 by giving the פסוק a different job.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not accept ״שָׂכִיר״ ״שָׂכִיר״.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The פסוק is needed to block a possible penalty on the slave sold by בית דין, not because the link is missing.

steps.title: Where is the pierced slave's release already stated?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from the earlier ברייתא, 'if it is about a נרצע, it is already stated,' and asks which פסוק that refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'If it is about a pierced slave, that is already stated.' Which פסוק is that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to one phrase in רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's ברייתא and asks where the תורה already teaches that a נרצע goes free at יובל. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא ruled out reading 'וְשָׁב אֶל מִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ' as being about a נרצע, because that case is 'already stated.' The ברייתא never named the פסוק, so the גמרא wants to find it.

keyTerms.meaning: A Hebrew slave whose ear was pierced because he chose to stay with his master after six years
'It is already stated.' Another פסוק already teaches this.

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: This quotes the ברייתא of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב from a few lines back.

phrases.english: If it is about a pierced slave, it is already stated.
What is it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: אִי בְּנִרְצָע – הֲרֵי כְּבָר אָמוּר. מַאי הִיא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to a detail inside the ברייתא from step 26 after the discussion in steps 27-28 ended.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק teaches that a נרצע goes free at יובל?

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the פסוק is about a pierced slave
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reasons that 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם אִישׁ אֶל אֲחֻזָּתוֹ' cannot be about the self-seller or the court-sold slave, since both are covered elsewhere. So it must be about a נרצע pierced a few years before יובל, and it teaches that יובל frees him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: 'And you shall return, each man to his land, and each man to his family.' Who is this פסוק about? If it is about a man who sold himself, that is already stated. If it is about a man sold by בית דין, that is already stated too. So the פסוק must be about a slave pierced two or three years before יובל, and it teaches that יובל sets him free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. It uses process of elimination to show that this פסוק is the source for a נרצע going free at יובל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of the other two kinds of Hebrew slave already has its own פסוק about יובל. The only case left for this פסוק is the נרצע. That makes it the place where his release is 'already stated.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is the פסוק speaking about?'
A man who sold himself as a slave because he was poor
A man sold by the court to pay back what he stole
The fiftieth year, when Hebrew slaves go free

steps.whyThisMatters: This is how we know that even a slave who chose to stay 'forever' still goes free at יובל.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:
"And you shall return, each man to his land,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:10

phrases.english: and each man to his family, etc."
What is the verse speaking about?

phrases.aramaic: אִי בְּמוֹכֵר עַצְמוֹ – הֲרֵי כְּבָר אָמוּר!
phrases.english: If it is about one who sells himself, it is already stated!
phrases.notes: That is 'עַד שְׁנַת הַיֹּבֵל יַעֲבֹד עִמָּךְ' (ויקרא 25:40).

phrases.aramaic: אִי בִּמְכָרוּהוּ בֵּית דִּין – הֲרֵי כְּבָר אָמוּר!
phrases.english: If it is about one whom the court sold, it is already stated!
So the verse is speaking about nothing

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בְּנִרְצַע שְׁתַּיִם וְשָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים לִפְנֵי הַיּוֹבֵל,
phrases.english: except one who was pierced two or three years before the יובל,
teaching that the יובל releases him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם אִישׁ אֶל אֲחֻזָּתוֹ' is about the נרצע, as shown by process of elimination.

steps.title: How do we know the פסוק means the pierced slave?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what in the פסוק itself shows that it is talking about a נרצע.
steps.simpleTranslation: What in the פסוק shows this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants a hint inside the words of the פסוק, not only process of elimination. This question sets up רבא בר שילא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Process of elimination tells us the פסוק is not needed for the other two slaves. It does not yet show any word in the פסוק that points to a נרצע. The גמרא asks for that word.

keyTerms.meaning: 'From where is it understood?' A request for the textual hint

phrases.english: From where is this understood?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the textual basis of the ברייתא's conclusion in step 30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which word in the פסוק points to a נרצע?

steps.title: The word 'man' points to piercing
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר שילא says the word 'אִישׁ' in the פסוק hints at something that applies only to a man and not to a woman. That is רציעה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר שילא said: The פסוק says 'man.' What applies to a man and not to a woman? It must be piercing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר שילא answers the question of step 31. The word 'אִישׁ' is the hint that the פסוק is about the נרצע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling oneself or being sold by בית דין does not need the word 'man' to explain it. רציעה is done only to a male slave and never to a Hebrew maidservant. So the word 'אִישׁ' points to the נרצע.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You must say.' Introduces the only possible answer
Piercing the slave's ear with an awl

phrases.english: Rava bar Sheila said:
The verse states: "man."
Which matter applies to a man
and does not apply to a woman?
You must say: this is piercing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר שֵׁילָא: אָמַר קְרָא: ״אִישׁ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31 with a specific word in the פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'אִישׁ' points to רציעה, which applies only to men.

steps.title: Why the court-sold case alone was not enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the תורה needed to write both the court-sold slave and the נרצע. If it had written only the court-sold slave, we might have thought the נרצע is penalized and never goes free.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה needed to write the man sold by בית דין, and it also needed to write the נרצע. If it had taught only the man sold by בית דין, we would say he goes free because his time to leave had not come yet. But the נרצע, whose time had come, we would say should be penalized.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the תורה needed two separate teachings about יובל, one for the court-sold slave and one for the נרצע. Here it shows the first half: why the court-sold case alone would not teach us about the נרצע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court-sold slave never had a chance to go free before יובל, so freeing him seems fair. The נרצע already had his chance after six years and turned it down. So we might have thought he deserves a penalty and stays a slave even past יובל.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was necessary.' Opens an explanation of why both teachings are needed
'It taught us'
'His time had come' to go free (after six years)
'Let us penalize him'

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 28. There the court-sold slave was the one who might be penalized, for his sin. Here the נרצע is the one who might be penalized, for turning down his freedom.

phrases.english: And it was necessary to write one whom the court sold,
and it was necessary to write a pierced slave.
For if it had taught us only one whom the court sold,
we would say he goes free because his time had not come;
but a pierced slave, whose time had come,
I would say: let us penalize him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיצְטְרִיךְ לְמִיכְתַּב מְכָרוּהוּ בֵּית דִּין, וְאִיצְטְרִיךְ לְמִיכְתַּב נִרְצָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that both sources are known (step 26 for the court-sold slave, step 30 for the נרצע), the גמרא explains why both are needed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court-sold case alone could not teach the נרצע, because the נרצע might have been penalized for turning down his freedom.

steps.title: Why the pierced case alone was not enough, so both are needed
steps.stepSummary: If the תורה had written only the נרצע, we might have thought he goes free because he already served six years, and that the court-sold slave, who did not, does not go free. So both teachings are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the תורה had taught only the נרצע, we would say he goes free because he already served six years. But the man sold by בית דין, who did not serve six years, we would say does not go free. So both teachings are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other half of its explanation and concludes that each teaching is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The נרצע already served the full six years, so letting him go at יובל seems fair. The court-sold slave sold close to יובל has not served six years, so we might have thought his master keeps him until six years are done. Each case has its own reason to think it is different, so neither can be learned from the other.

keyTerms.meaning: 'He served him six' years
'I would say not'
'It is necessary.' Both teachings are needed

steps.whatToRemember: יובל frees every Hebrew slave. The court-sold slave's release comes from 'ושב אל משפחתו' and the נרצע's release comes from 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם אִישׁ'. The תורה needed both, because each case had its own reason we might have thought he stays a slave.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only a pierced slave,
we would say he goes free because he served him six,
but one whom the court sold,
who did not serve him six,
I would say: not.
So it is necessary.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אַשְׁמְעִינַן נִרְצָע, מִשּׁוּם דַּעֲבַד לֵיהּ שֵׁשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided explanation begun in step 33.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Neither case can be learned from the other, so the תורה had to teach both the court-sold slave and the נרצע going free at יובל.

steps.title: Both 'And you shall return' and 'forever' are needed, part one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the תורה had to write both 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם' and 'לְעוֹלָם' about the נרצע. If it had written only 'לְעוֹלָם', we would think he serves his whole life.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed to write 'and you shall return', and it was needed to write 'forever'. If the תורה had written only 'forever', I would think it means really forever. So the תורה wrote 'and you shall return'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new 'both are needed' argument. This time it is about two פסוקים that deal with the same person, the נרצע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לְעוֹלָם' (שמות) says the נרצע serves 'forever'. Read alone, that sounds like his whole life. 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם' (ויקרא) is needed to show that יובל still sets him free.

keyTerms.meaning: It was needed (both sources are necessary)
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה
Forever, said about the נרצע in שמות
I would have thought (the mistaken first idea)

phrases.english: And it was needed to write 'and you shall return',
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:10

phrases.english: and it was needed to write 'forever'.
phrases.notes: שמות 21:6, said about the slave whose ear is pierced.

phrases.english: For if the Merciful One had written only 'forever',
I would have said it means really forever,
so the Merciful One wrote 'and you shall return'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'both are needed' pattern as steps 33-34, now for two פסוקים about the נרצע himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'לְעוֹלָם' alone would mean a lifetime of service, so 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם' is needed to free the נרצע at יובל.

steps.title: Both are needed, part two: 'forever' means until יובל
steps.stepSummary: If only 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם' were written, we might think a נרצע who already served six years after the piercing goes free then. So 'לְעוֹלָם' teaches that he serves until יובל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the תורה had written only 'and you shall return', I would think that applies only where he has not served six years. But where he has served six, his end should not be stricter than his start: just as at the start he served six, so at the end he serves six. So the תורה teaches 'forever', meaning the 'forever' of יובל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other half: why 'לְעוֹלָם' is needed even though we have 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם'. This closes the 'both are needed' argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without 'לְעוֹלָם', we might reason that the pierced stage should not be harsher than the first six-year sale. Then he would go free after six years or at יובל, whichever comes first. 'לְעוֹלָם' rules this out: he serves all the way until יובל, even if that takes more than six years.

keyTerms.meaning: This applies only (to a limited case)
His end should not be stricter than his beginning
It teaches us (the conclusion)
The 'forever' of יובל, meaning until יובל

steps.whatToRemember: 'לְעוֹלָם' and 'וְשַׁבְתֶּם' work together. The נרצע does not serve for life and does not leave after six years. He serves until יובל.
steps.confusionAlert: 'לְעוֹלָם' here does not mean 'for his whole life'. The גמרא reads it as 'until יובל'.

phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written only 'and you shall return',
I would have said: this applies only
where he did not serve six years,
phrases.notes: Six years counted from when he was pierced.

phrases.english: but where he did serve six years,
his end should not be stricter than his beginning;
just as his beginning was six years,
so too his end should also be six years.
So it teaches us: 'forever'
means the 'forever' of יובל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second half of the 'both are needed' argument that step 35 started.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both words are needed, so together they teach that the נרצע serves until יובל, no more and no less.

steps.title: Then who does not learn 'hired worker' from 'hired worker'?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק showed that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב may accept the 'שָׂכִיר' 'שָׂכִיר' link after all. So the גמרא asks again which תנא rejects it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, who is the תנא who does not learn 'hired worker' from 'hired worker'?
steps.whatsHappening: The word 'rather' tells us the earlier attempt to name the תנא did not work. The גמרא asks the question again and gets ready for a new answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer was רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, because he needed a separate פסוק to free the slave sold by בית דין at יובל. רב נחמן בר יצחק showed that the פסוק was needed anyway, to block a penalty, so that proof failed. The side discussion about the נרצע is now finished, and the search starts over.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (the earlier idea is dropped)
A sage from the time of the משנה
Hired worker, a word used about the עבד עברי in two places
Learning a law by comparing the same word in two places

phrases.english: Rather, who is the תנא
who does not learn 'hired worker' from 'hired worker'?
phrases.notes: This is the גזירה שוה that compares the word שָׂכִיר in two פסוקים about the slave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the question of step 25, since רב נחמן בר יצחק in step 28 rejected the proof that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב is that תנא. The side discussion in steps 29-36 is finished.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא rejects the גזירה שוה of 'שָׂכִיר' 'שָׂכִיר'.

steps.title: It is רבי, as a ברייתא teaches
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the תנא is רבי and begins to bring a ברייתא as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי, as it is taught in a ברייתא:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names רבי as the תנא. It then sets up the next move, a ברייתא that will show this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the answer is only a name. The ברייתא that comes next must show that רבי does not use the 'שָׂכִיר' 'שָׂכִיר' comparison.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה

phrases.english: It is רבי,
phrases.notes: This means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a ברייתא:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 37 and starts quoting a ברייתא as proof.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תנא who does not learn 'שָׂכִיר' 'שָׂכִיר' is רבי, as a ברייתא will show.
